Fazlul Karim with Khandaker Aminul Huq, Advocates ----- For the Appellant.

Vs

full_judgment:
4. The defendant entered appearance and filed written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable and is barred by limitation and that the plea of transfer in favour of plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 for alleged construction without consent of the plaintiffs in the suit premises and notice by the RAJUK for demolishing of the house are false. It was asserted that the defendant is an English Medium School of Dhaka with about 500 students who are prosecuting their studies from Play Group to 'O' Level and they took lease from the plaintiff No.1 as per agreement dated 12-3-90 for a period of 2 years and the same was renewed by another agreement for a period of 3 years on 19- 3-92 and then another fresh agreement was entered into for 6 years and they acquired right to hold the suit premises up to March, 2001. The defendant was 'paying rent regularly and subsequently plaintiff No.1 refused to accept the rent from the defendant and hence defendant filed House Rent Case No. 15 of 1998 before the Court of Rent Controller and has been paying rent therein. The plaintiff No.1 also received some payment from the office of the Rent Controller and it was further asserted that the plaintiffs do not require the premises for reconstruction or for bonafide requirement. It was further asserted that the notice under section 106 of the TP Act was not a legal one as it was served before the expiry of the lease period. The oral gift by the plaintiff No. 1 in favour of plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 is not legal and prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 7. Heard Mr Fazlul Karim with Mr Khandaker Aminul Huq, the learned Advocates appearing for the defendant-appellant and Mr Golam Arshad, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, perused the paper book, including the plaint, written statement, deposition of the witnesses and the exhibits. Mr Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the suit is not maintainable in absence of a proper notice under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act prior to the notice under section 106 of the said Act. He also submits that the trial Court acted illegally in holding that the defendant is a defaulter having misconceived the provision of depositing rent as provided under the provision of Rent Control Ordinance. He lastly, submits that the damages decreed by the court below for the plaintiffs are against the provision of law. 

 8. On the other hand, Mr Golam Arshad, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, submits that in order to get protection against the eviction the defendant must show up-to-date payment till the final decree and since the defendant failed to show that they paid rent up to date the court below has rightly decreed the suit. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the respondent has referred to the case of Ramjan Ali Mistry vs Md Hedayetullah reported in 31 DLR (AD) 183 wherein it was held: 

 9. He has also referred to the case of Nowab Meah vs NurNahar Begum reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 74, the case of Profulla Kumar Chakraborty vs Anil Prashad Choudhury and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 55, and the case of AKM Shamsuddin and others vs Altafuddin Ahmed reported in 43 DLR (AD) 230. He next submits that deposit of rent in favour of previous landlord will not protect the tenant from being defaulter and from being evicted as such. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Basiruddin Ahmed and others vs Dhirendra Mohan Das and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 191. He further submits that in paragraph 9 of the plaint a definite case was made out by the plaintiffs that the plaintiff No. 1 gifted the property in favour of plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3. Moreover Exhibits, 5 and 6 showed that notices by the RAJUK were also served upon the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and moreover, Exhibit 4 dated 8-9-91 also showed that the suit premises was mutated in the name of plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 but even then defendant did not care to pay any rent to the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and therefore, the trial Court rightly held that the defendant is a defaulter. He next submits that the onus is upon the defendant to state under what circumstances he made the payment before the House Rent Controller and whether the Rent Controller accepted and gave permission to deposit the rent. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Abul Layes vs Anwara Khatun and legal representative. Abu Sayed Ahmed and others reported in 29 DLR (SC) 13. He submits that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act has been duly and legally served upon the defendant and in view of the decision in the case of Sultana vs Syed Ahmed reported in 19 DLR 42 the trial Court has rightly held that the tenancy was terminated by proper and legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and that it has been properly served, as required by law. He lastly submits that the court has believed Exhibits 8 to 11, the notice under section 106 and the postal receipt and acknowledgment receipt and committed no illegality in decreeing the suit. 

 10. It appears that in the written statement and in the deposition by DW 1, it has been asserted that after refusal to receive the rent by the plaintiff No. 1 defendant started to deposit the rent to House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 15 of 1998. It is now admitted that the rent case ended in dismissal and Miscellaneous Appeal was filed before the District Judge Dhaka being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 31 of 2003 and in that case defendant also prayed for provisional permission to deposit the rent but the permission was refused. It further appears that against notice issued by RAJUK for demolishing the suit premises, the defendant filed a suit ie Title Suit No. 99 of 1999, praying for a permanent injunction and the prayer having been refused, they filed Civil Revision No. 3625 of 2000 in this court and the matter went up to the Appellate Division where the prayer for injunction was refused in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 274 of 2001. It appears that there is no order by the Rent Controller in the Rent Case No. 15 of 1998 that the defendant deposited rent as per provision of section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1991 but even that Miscellaneous Case ended in dismissal and they did not make any payment after September, 2002 and therefore, admittedly the defendant-appellant did not pay any rent either to plaintiff No.1 or to plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 after the dismissal of the Rent Case No. 15 of 1998 and therefore, the moment they did not pay the rent they became defaulters and disentitled to get any relief from being evicted as a tenant. Moreover, the lease agreement admittedly ended after March 2001 and since then the appellant is no longer tenant of the plaintiffs. Further it appears that although a definite case was made out 'in the plaint itself that the suit land has been gifted in favour of plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 but no attempt has been made either to investigate about such transfer or making payment of the rent in favour of plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and therefore payment of rent even if in the name of plaintiff No. 1 will be no ground to save the defendant from being defaulter in view of the decision as referred to above by the learned Advocate for the respondents reported in 36 DLR (AD) 191. It further appears from Exhibits 5 and 6 that the trial Court rightly held that RAJUK served notice upon the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 to demolish the premises as it was very old and dilapidated. PW 2 has proved that the defendant made unauthorised construction on the suit land beyond the plan of 'the building and the plaintiff made out a case of re-building also and therefore, the trial Court committed no illegality in considering this aspect of the case of bonafide requirement for the purpose of re-building and we find that the court below has not committed any illegality believing the case of rebuilding in favour of the plaintiffs. 

 11. Mr Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has referred to section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, and submits that since the plaintiffs did not serve 6 months' notice for forefeiture the notice under section 106 alone is illegal and consequently, the suit is not maintainable. Mr Golam Arshad, the learned Advocate, has referred to section 18 of the Rent Control Ordinance and submits that this provision shall apply notwithstanding any provision of Transfer of Property Act or Contract Act and notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act has been legally served for terminating the tenancy. We find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondents and since the agreement in question is not a registered one it must be held to be a tenancy for month to month. Mr Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, lastly referred to a decision in the case' of Raja Mohammad Amir Ahmad Khan vs Municipal Board of Sitapur and another reported in AIR 1965 SC 1923 in support of his contention that the principle embodied in section 111 (g) is equally applicable to tenancies. We do not find that this decision has any manner of application in this case. 'He has referred to the case of Chandra Nath Mukherjee vs Chulai Pashi and another reported in AIR 1960 (Cal) 40. In that case it was held that the defendants were non- agricultural tenants within the meaning of that Act by virtue of section 88 read with section 9, six months' notice was essential to determine the tenancy and without such notice no decree for ejectment could be passed in plaintiff's favour. We do not find that this decision has any manner of application in this case inasmuch as the present tenancy is not for agricultural purpose. We do not also find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that a notice under section 111(g) ought to have been served before notice under 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 13. During hearing of the appeal application under Order XLI rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been filed by the appellant for admission of additional evidence showing payment of electricity bill and the WASA bills and the respondent also filed another application for accepting additional evidence filing the order sheet of Miscellanies Appeal No. 31 of 2003 showing that the rent deposit case ended in dismissal and in the appeal the defendant prayed for provisional permission to deposit rent which was refused.
